en: Record of Temples and Pagodas:
In the summer of the third year of the Guihai year of the Wuzong reign of the Tang dynasty, I, along with my colleagues Zhang Jun Xifu and Shan Ji, served together in office.
Biqiu Zhengjun’s symbolic dreams were again linked to his appointment in the office of the immortals.
On a day of leisure, he visited Daxingshan Temple and consequently asked:
The *New Records of the Two Capitals* and the *Record of Sightseeing* omit many details; thus,
I have briefly summarized my search for the temples of the two streets over approximately ten days,
beginning with Xingshan Monastery on the eastern street.
Those items not fully recorded in the two accounts were compiled separately;
he then traveled to Ci'en Monastery.
When he first learned that the government officials were seizing the temple and the monastic community was in a state of disarray,
he made some general inquiries regarding one or two matters.
The Master [Daoxuan] recorded the traces of the paintings beneath the stupa;
his travels to this place were thereafter cut short.
Three years later.
While serving my official duties in the capitals of Chang’an and Luoyang, and later as the Governor of Ancheng,
I returned to the capital in the seventh year of the Dazhong era.
Of the books I had kept during my six cycles of the sexagenary calendar spent away from court, half were completely ruined or lost.
In the old records, I saw that when he visited the temple with his two deceased fathers,
their tears flowed like dripping blood;
the joyful events of that time are now far beyond reach.
I have further revised and corrected them,
yet they are barely sufficient to continue the transmission;
nevertheless, five or six parts in ten have been lost.
Subsequently, it was compiled into two fascicles and transmitted among the sons of Śākyamuni.
Duan Chengshi, courtesy name Ke Gu, was a native of Dongmu.
In the Jinggong Ward is the Daxingshan Temple;
the temple takes two characters from "Daxing" (Great Flourishing) and one character from the ward name to form its name.
The *Xinji* states:
"The statue of King Udayana was burned by fire at the beginning of the Zongzhang era."
According to records from the Liang dynasty, the Yutian (Udayana) image was in Jingzhou during that period;
therefore, the claim that it was moved from the Taicheng palace to this temple during the Sui dynasty is incorrect.
Furthermore, there is now a sandalwood image [there as well].
The craftsmanship of the open eyes is rather crude;
it is still somewhat erroneous.
Before the stupa of the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra, there are many aged pines.
If the year begins early, officials shall cut its branches to fashion "dragon bones" for praying for rain;
this is likely the intention behind the Tripitaka Master's subjugation of the dragon.
That tree must surely possess spiritual power. On the rear wall of the Incense Hall,
the painter Liang Qia painted a pair of pine trees during the Yuanhe era.
It has slightly departed from conventional styles.
The craftsmanship of the clay sculptures in the Mañjuśrī Hall is extremely exquisite.
On the exterior walls are gilt-bronze paintings.
The *Amanasikāra-sūtra* brought from the Western Regions by Amoghavajra himself is housed within the Sandalwood Image Hall;
it contains both the *sūtras for specific times* and the *sūtras for non-specific times*.
The monk said: "I copied it using vermilion ink on silk and placed it within a lacquered shrine."
These are relics from the Sui dynasty.
Behind the temple there was formerly a curved pond.
When Amoghavajra was nearing the end of his life, he said:
Suddenly it dried up completely;
when Chan Master Weikuan arrived and took up residence there,
the spring flowed again due to heavy rains.
White lotus algae grew there spontaneously;
now it has once again become dry land.
To the south of the eastern corridor is the hall of Master Su.
In the courtyard were four saplings of green paulownia,
which had been planted by Lady Su herself.
During the Yuanhe era, many high ministers and officials frequented this garden.
In summer, the paulownia tree exudes a sap that stains people's clothes like axle grease;
it cannot be washed out.
Looking to the left, there is an image of a clam.
According to ancient tradition,
it is said that the Sui Emperor was fond of clams.
In all his meals, he invariably included the flavor of clams;
these numbered more than several tens of millions.
Suddenly, there was one clam.
He struck it as he had done before;
the Emperor marveled at this and placed it upon his desk.
One night, it emitted a light.
When it was clear that the meat had detached itself,
inside there were images of one Buddha and two Bodhisattvas.
The Emperor, filled with grief and remorse, vowed never again to eat clams.
This is not the Khotanese jade image from the reign of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty.
It is one chi seven cun in height and slightly over one cun in width,
depicting one Buddha and four bodhisattvas.
A single immortal, a whole piece of jade perfected;
like cut lard without flaw,
its glossy luster seems as if it were dripping.
The Tiandwang Pavilion was constructed during the Changqing era.
Originally, it stood within the Chunming Gate.
It shares a wall with the Southern Palace;
its scale is the greatest in the world.
In the second year of the Tahe era, an imperial decree ordered it to be moved to this temple.
When it was dismantled,
five hundred bolts of cloth and several dozen jars of lacquer were found within its belly.
Today, the images of the local deities have fallen into ruin.
Only the Red Tower of Anguo Temple in Changle Ward was spared by the Heavenly King;
it was a dance pavilion from when Emperor Ruizong was still a prince.
The Dongcheon-ya (East Zen Monastery),
also known as the Mota-ya (Wooden Pagoda Monastery),
has five walls along its northern and western corridors.
The monk Sidao, a disciple of Wu Daoxuan, painted the eight classes of Śakra and Brahmā deities;
though no colors were applied,
they still preserve the classical style and formal integrity.
The statue of Hārītī and the clay image of Crown Prince Wenhui within Guangming Temple both exhibit gestures and postures as lifelike as those of living beings.
The artisan was named Li Xiù.
It was a mountain courtyard with ancient trees and lofty mounds.
Secluded as a mountain valley,
it was at that time a mound of earth established as the courtyard of the Venerable Lin, the Abbot;
there stood a single trunk of a cypress tree with tassels.
The branches of the *qú* tree spread out and cover it;
more than ten people sit beneath it.
Zhaojinggong Temple in Changlefang was established in the third year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
The original record states it was Hongshan Temple;
it was renamed [the current name] in the eighteenth year.
On the eastern wall inside the south central gate:
Wu Daoxuan’s white-line painting of the Transformation of Hell possesses a vigorous and wrathful brush power;
its manifested forms are dark and grotesque.
Beholding it, one cannot help but feel one's hair stand on end;
it is the most successful passage among the paintings of the Wu school,
located beneath the western corridor of the Sanjie Courtyard.
Fan Changshou painted the Transformation of the Western Paradise and the sixteen pairs of attendants at the Jewel Pond;
the pond was particularly exquisite.
Upon gazing at it intently, [one could see...]
I noticed that water had entered deeply;
on the wall above the gate of the courtyard,
there were white-painted trees and rocks.
He bears a striking resemblance to Yan Lide.
I brought with me a draft copy of the "Hengtian Ci" (Song of Traveling through Heaven) by Lide;
upon comparison, they were found to be no different.
To the south of the inner gate of the three gates in the western section,
Wu Sheng painted dragons and brushed the beards of the Heavenly Kings.
The calligraphy is as firm as iron.
There is a celestial maiden holding an incense burner,
who steals a glance as if wishing to speak.
In the center of the Huayan Hall stands a bronze standing statue of Rocana six feet in height;
it is of ancient style and exquisite craftsmanship.
Beneath the pagoda are three pecks and four sheng of śarīra.
At the time of the stupa’s relocation,
the monk Shouxing established a ritual site (*maṇḍala*) and brought forth the śarīra,
allowing the officials and commoners to behold them.
Before the chanting and praise had concluded,
śarīras appeared covering the ground;
the men and women did not dare to tread upon them.
They all went outside the temple.
Master Shou then constructed small clay stupas and wooden stupas,
numbering nearly one hundred thousand, in which he enshrined them.
Currently, several tens of thousands still remain there.
The temple contains more than six hundred small silver elephants and one golden Buddha statue several feet in height.
There is a large silver elephant over six feet in height,
exquisitely crafted in an ancient style.
There is also a small folding screen depicting the Heart Sutra, its characters inlaid with the seven precious gems.
It was placed within a precious casket,
upon which various colored pearls and white pearls were set in a dense,
variegated pattern.
During the rebellion of An Lushan,
officials took refuge in this temple.
There are fifteen panels with thirty lines each on the folding screens.
The postscript states:
The initiator was the Minister of the Household (Sima), Hengcun;
the patron for the fulfillment of the vow was the Senior Pillar of State (Shangzhuguo), Suofubo Xi.
Zhen De, a Shangzhuguo (High Pillar of State),
fashioned golden tablets for the sake of sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm;
Shanji suspected them to be foreign objects.
Regarding the juniper tree described in the *Youmujì*:
it was felled during the Taizhong era to serve as timber for the imperial palace.
It stood at Baoying Temple in Daozheng Ward, where Han Gan [painted its likeness].
He was a native of Lantian.
In his youth, he often served as a wine deliveryman for a tavern.
Wang Juyong and his brothers had not yet achieved their fortunes.
Every time he roamed about after purchasing wine,
he would constantly collect debts at the royal palace and playfully draw figures of men and horses on the ground.
The Right Vice-Director was deeply absorbed in his contemplation of painting;
finding its conception extraordinary,
he completed it and presented him with twenty thousand coins.
He was made to study painting for over ten years.
The figures of Śakra, Brahmā, and the celestial maidens currently in the temple are all lifelike portraits drawn by Qi Gong’s former concubines, Xiao Xiao and others.
In the temple there is a hanging scroll depicting the Descent from Heaven by Han Gan.
Maitreya wears a purple *kāṣāya*,
with a Bodhisattva gazing upward on his right side and two lions.
It is as if entering a divine realm.
Within the northwest corner courtyard,
there is a copy of Yan Lugu’s Preface written by Huaisu.
Praise by Vice-Minister Zhang Wei and Magistrate Qian Qi for the Transformation of the Verse on Form from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
painted by Wu Daoxuan on the eastern wall of the dining hall at Pusa Temple in Pingkang Ward.
These verses were personally inscribed by [the Master] during the Wu dynasty;
the calligraphy is vigorous and forceful,
like the tearing out of a demon’s hair.
Next, on the wall, he painted the immortal Ribhu;
his celestial robes fluttered as if stirred by a wind that filled the entire surface of the wall.
On the rear wall of the inner aisle within the Buddha Hall,
Wu Daoxuan painted scenes from the *Xiuzai Jing* (Sutra on the Elimination of Calamities).
The trees and rocks are depicted with ancient, rugged majesty.
During the Yuanhe era, the Emperor wished to relocate it;
fearing its destruction,
he issued an imperial edict.
A painter was selected to execute the work:
the Transformation of Vimalakīrti on the inner recess of the east wall within the Buddha Hall.
Śāriputra’s elbows were bent and his knees turned outward.
Toward the end of the Yuanhe era,
the lay lecturer-monk Wenshu restored it.
The calligraphy has been exhausted.
Regarding the architectural layout of the temple, the bell tower is situated in the east;
however, in this particular temple, it is because the residence of the Right Seat Minister Lin Fu was located to the east.
Therefore, a bell tower was constructed to the west.
Within the temple were Gao Lishi’s tortoise-shell whip and Gao Lishi and his consort Wang’s seven-jeweled canopy.
The temple master Yuanjing was widely learned in the Buddhist tradition.
According to historical accounts,
whenever the Right Seat Li reached his birthday, [the following occurred].
He constantly invited the monks of this monastery to his residence to partake in vegetarian feasts.
Among them was a certain monk named Yi, who once sighed in praise of the Buddha.
He donated one set of saddles, which,
when sold, fetched a material value of seventy thousand [coins].
Furthermore, the monk Sengguang possessed a great reputation.
He recited the sutra for several years.
Next, he was to offer praise to the Buddha;
therefore, he gazed intently at the merit of the person seated to his right.
Hoping to obtain a generous shroud,
he emerged from beneath the curtain after the meal with a colorful basket and a fragrant silk napkin as a base,
only to find within it a single object resembling a decayed nail, several inches in length.
The monk returned home disappointed and filled with remorse;
after several days, he reflected that the great minister could not possibly have deceived him.
He then took it to the Western Market and showed it to a Sogdian merchant.
Upon seeing it, the merchant was struck with amazement and said:
"How could a superior person possess such an object?
You must have sold it at a price that did not exceed its value.
Let me test you by asking for a hundred thousand."
The Hu man laughed loudly and said,
"Not yet. Speak further with all your heart."
He increased the price to five hundred thousand;
the foreigner said,
"This is worth ten million."
He then gave it to him.
The monk inquired as to its name,
and [the donor] replied, "This is precious bone."
Furthermore, there was previously a monk in the monastery whose name and surname were not mentioned;
he constantly carried bundles of straw mats on his back.
He sat and slept beneath the two corridors of the monastery,
refusing to reside within the temple compound for several years.
When the administrators of the monastery urged him to take up residence there,
he said, "Do you weary of me? That very evening,
he consequently burned his body with a bundle of straw.
When morning came, there was nothing but ashes;
not even the odor of blood or fat remained.
Only then did the multitude realize he was an extraordinary person.
He then fashioned an image out of ash,
which remains today above the Buddha hall;
he is popularly known as the "Straw-Binding Master."
Guangzhai Temple in the Guangzhai Ward: The Pu-xian Hall was originally the Empress Wuhou’s dressing chamber.
When the grapes hung with fruit, she would visit this hall.
Today, the Wei-chi (Yuchi) murals within the hall possess many extraordinary features.
On the four walls are murals of flayed white bones;
the artisan’s conception is extremely perilous.
Furthermore, there are three transformed demonesses.
The figures appear as if emerging from the wall;
furthermore, the colors of the Buddha’s halo blend so harmoniously that they dazzle the eyes, forming a lecture hall.
On the eastern wall, before the Buddha’s seat, the brocade is like a fragment of an ancient banner.
The western wall presses against it, making it appear towering and imposing.
This is Jingyu Monastery in Xuanyang Ward; it was originally the residence of Empress Taimu.
A monk of the monastery said:
Outside the gate of the third courtyard is the place where Emperor Shendiao shot peacocks;
above it, coiled snakes and filthy smoke are fearsome to behold.
The trees and rocks along the eastern corridor are rugged and strange; even eminent monks find them strange.

At Chongji Temple in Chaoguo Fang, behind the temple, there are six items: a dragon-patterned brocade robe woven by Empress Wu and embroidered garments. This is the second courtyard from the south in the eastern enclosure.
There are the Kāṣāya Hall and Mañjuśrī Hall constructed by Vinaya Master Xuán;
there are several pine trees that are most extraordinary.
Outside the gate of the Jìngtǔyúan (Pure Land Cloister) in Chóngshèng Fāng (Venerable Sage Ward), Zásèng Sī (Zásèng Temple).
It is traditionally said that one night, Wu Zongzi painted while holding a candle and intoxicated;
upon seeing his own work, he clenched his fists in dismay and was struck with horror.
Inside the monastery gate, Lu Lengqia constantly studied the style of Wu.
Wu also bestowed upon him manual instructions.
Consequently, he completed the painting of the three gates of Zongchi Temple while it was still half-finished;
Wu greatly praised his work.
He said to the man:
"If you have not obtained the heart-essence of the Laṅkāvatāra, your practice will be too arduous; how can it endure?"
He passed away after completing the paintings.
Because the Ci’en Monastery was impure, he established a new monastery on that site;
it consisted of some ten or more courtyards.
In total, there were one thousand eight hundred and ninety-seven rooms.
By imperial decree, three hundred monks were ordained.
This was the beginning of the period when the Tripitaka Master returned from the Western Regions.

By imperial decree, Prince Daozong of Jiangxia, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, was appointed to arrange the music of the nine regions to welcome the scriptures and images into the temple;
there were over a thousand decorated carriages in total.
The Emperor ascended to the Anfu Gate to observe it.
Taisong had once bestowed upon the Tripiṭaka Master a patchwork robe (*nā*) worth over a hundred pieces of gold;
its craftsmanship showed no trace of needle or thread.
The chestnut tree and white peony within the temple were planted by the hand of the Venerable Fǎlì.
